By the Novikov-Yakovenko theorem and Lemma 12: for the chosen  $ T_0 $ and sufficiently small  $ \varepsilon $ there exists a universal constant  $ N $ such that on each block of length  $ T_0 $ the number of intersections of the trajectory with the surfaces  $ \{l = \pm \varepsilon\} $ does not exceed  $ N $.

Consequently, the number of entries into  $ U_{\varepsilon}(H) $ on one block is at most N/2. Here an entry into  $ U_{\varepsilon}(H) $ means the initial moment of each continuous interval of stay in  $ U_{\varepsilon}(H) $.

This is possible because  $ T_* $ in Lemma 10 can be taken arbitrarily small. Next fix  $ \varepsilon \leq \varepsilon_*\big(\delta\big) $ so that the bound on the number of intersections and the exit time estimate are applicable.

More precisely, the order of choice is as follows: first pick a small range for  $ \varepsilon $, then obtain the corresponding estimate N from the Novikov–Yakovenko theorem, then choose  $ T_{*} $ so that (18) holds, and then, if necessary, decrease the admissible  $ \varepsilon $ according to Lemma 10. The estimate N does not increase from such a decrease.
Step 5: good block, case 1. Consider a good block, i.e., a block for which  $ v_j < \gamma/8 $. Consider the next entry into  $ U_\varepsilon(H) $.

First case: the entry occurs outside  $ W_\delta $. At the moment of entry  $ x_0 \notin W_\delta $, hence by Lemma 10 the trajectory leaves  $ U_\varepsilon(H) $ in time at most  $ T_\star $. It does not matter whether it later enters  $ W_\delta $ during this interval or not: Lemma 10 gives the answer independently of a subsequent entry into  $ W_\delta $.

Step 6: good block, case 2. Second case: the entry occurs inside  $ W_\delta $. Let the trajectory first stay in  $ W_\delta $ for time  $ \tau_i $, then leave  $ W_\delta $ and, as in the first case, leave  $ U_\varepsilon(H) $ in time at most  $ T_\star $. Therefore for each such entry we obtain a contribution not exceeding  $ \tau_i + T_\star $.

This is precisely why Lemma 12 is used: the number of intersections with the boundaries  $ \{l = \pm\varepsilon\} $ on each block is bounded above, so the trajectory cannot oscillate arbitrarily many times between the boundaries.
